summary: Describes the BLAKE2 cryptographic hash function and provides the specification and C source code. BLAKE2b suits 64-bit platforms and BLAKE2s smaller ones. It can be keyed directly, so it also works as a MAC.

plainLanguage.summary: BLAKE2 turns any amount of data into a short, fixed-length value. This document describes the algorithm and gives C source code for it. There are two versions: one for 64-bit computers and a smaller one for other machines. A secret key can be built in, so the same function also checks that a message was not altered.

subtitle: A hash function with a built-in key, so one algorithm covers both checksums and message authentication.

tldr.problem: Applications need a fast hash function for checksums, signatures and message authentication, and they want a secure one that does not need a separate HMAC wrapper around it.
tldr.mechanism: BLAKE2 compresses the input in fixed-size blocks through a mixing function run for 12 rounds in BLAKE2b and 10 in BLAKE2s, and it takes an optional secret key as its first block.
tldr.outcome: The result is a digest of any length the caller chooses, from 1 to 64 bytes in BLAKE2b and 1 to 32 bytes in BLAKE2s, and the RFC also supplies reference C code and worked traces.

today: RFC 7693 is an Informational document published in November 2015 as an independent submission. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is a published specification rather than an Internet Standard.

sections.title: Two Versions of One Hash Function
sections.content:
The BLAKE2 cryptographic hash function was designed by Jean-Philippe Aumasson, Samuel Neves, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn and Christian Winnerlein. A hash function turns input data of any length into a short fixed-length value, called a digest. This document describes BLAKE2 and makes the algorithm specification and C source code available to the Internet community.

BLAKE2 comes in two basic flavors. BLAKE2b, or just BLAKE2, is optimized for 64-bit platforms and produces digests of any size between 1 and 64 bytes. BLAKE2s is optimized for 8- to 32-bit platforms and produces digests of any size between 1 and 32 bytes. Both are believed to be highly secure and to perform well on any platform, in software or in hardware.

BLAKE2 does not require a separate HMAC construction for keyed message authentication, because it has a keying mechanism built in. The document says BLAKE2 may be used by digital signature algorithms and by message authentication and integrity protection mechanisms, in applications such as Public Key Infrastructure, secure communication protocols, cloud storage, intrusion detection, forensic suites and version control systems.

Compared with the Secure Hash Algorithm family and HMAC-SHA described in RFC 6234, the document presents the BLAKE2 suite as a more efficient alternative. BLAKE2s-128 is described as especially suited as a fast and more secure drop-in replacement for MD5 and HMAC-MD5 in legacy applications, where RFC 6151 sets out the security considerations for those two algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: BLAKE2 turns any amount of data into a short, fixed-length value, and the document gives the algorithm and C source code for it. There are two versions: one for 64-bit computers and a smaller one for other machines.

sections.title: Parameters, Constants and the Parameter Block
sections.content:
The parameters differ between the two flavors. BLAKE2b uses 64-bit words, 12 rounds and blocks of 128 bytes, with digests from 1 to 64 bytes, keys from 0 to 64 bytes, and inputs of fewer than 2^128 bytes. BLAKE2s uses 32-bit words, 10 rounds and blocks of 64 bytes, with digests from 1 to 32 bytes, keys from 0 to 32 bytes, and inputs of fewer than 2^64 bytes. The rotation constants used by the mixing function are (32, 24, 16, 63) for BLAKE2b and (16, 12, 8, 7) for BLAKE2s.

Several named values appear throughout the algorithm. IV[0..7] is the Initialization Vector, a constant. SIGMA[0..9] holds the message word permutations. The parameter block p[0..7] defines the hash and key sizes. m[0..15] holds the sixteen words of a single message block. h[0..7] is the internal state of the hash. d[0..dd-1] are the padded input blocks, each of bb bytes. t is the message byte offset at the end of the current block, and f is a flag that marks the last block.

Byte streams are interpreted as words in little-endian order, with the least significant byte first. The parameter block consists of eight words whose first word is p[0] = 0x0101kknn and whose other seven words are zero. The nn byte gives the hash size in bytes and the kk byte gives the key size in bytes, with kk set to 00 for unkeyed hashing. Bytes 2 and 3 are set as 01 and all other bytes are set as zero. The earlier BLAKE2 paper defines additional optional features, such as salting, personalized hashes and tree hashing, which use fields in the parameter block that this document does not define.

The Initialization Vector is defined as IV[i] = floor(2^w * frac(sqrt(prime(i+1)))), where prime(i) is the i-th prime number (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19) and sqrt(x) is the square root of x. The BLAKE2b IV is the same as the SHA-512 IV, and the BLAKE2s IV is the same as the SHA-256 IV. The message schedule SIGMA holds ten permutations of the sixteen message words, and for BLAKE2b the two extra permutations needed for rounds 10 and 11 repeat SIGMA[0..1].
sections.plainLanguage: The two versions differ in the size of the numbers they work with and in how many rounds they run. The document fixes these values in a table and stores the chosen digest size and key size in the first word of a parameter block.

sections.title: The Mixing Function and the Compression Function
sections.content:
The mixing function G takes two input words, x and y, and mixes them into four words of a working vector v[0..15]. It adds, exclusive-ors and rotates in a fixed order: v[a] := (v[a] + v[b] + x) mod 2^w, then v[d] := (v[d] ^ v[a]) >>> R1, then v[c] := (v[c] + v[d]) mod 2^w, then v[b] := (v[b] ^ v[c]) >>> R2, and the same four steps again with y and the rotations R3 and R4. The full modified vector is returned.

The compression function F takes as its arguments the state vector h, a message block m (the last block is padded with zeros to the full block size if required), a 2w-bit offset counter t and a final block indicator flag f. It returns a new state vector. It first copies the state into the first half of a local vector v[0..15] and the Initialization Vector into the second half. It then exclusive-ors the low word of the offset into v[12] and the high word into v[13], and, when the flag marks the last block, inverts all the bits of v[14].

The cryptographic mixing then runs for r rounds, 12 for BLAKE2b and 10 for BLAKE2s. Each round selects a message word permutation from SIGMA, using SIGMA[i mod 10], and applies the mixing function eight times to pairs of message words. When the rounds are done, the two halves of the working vector are exclusive-ored into the state, producing the new state vector.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block of the message goes through one function that mixes the hash so far together with that block. Inside it, a shorter routine called the mixing function adds, exclusive-ors and rotates numbers, and the whole sequence is repeated for a fixed number of rounds.

sections.title: Producing a Digest, With or Without a Key
sections.content:
The key and the data input are split and padded into dd message blocks d[0..dd-1], each consisting of 16 words, or bb bytes. If a secret key is used, it is padded with zero bytes and set as d[0]; otherwise d[0] is the first data block. The final data block d[dd-1] is also padded with zeros to bb bytes. The number of blocks is therefore dd = ceil(kk / bb) + ceil(ll / bb), except that in the special case of an unkeyed empty message, dd is still set to 1 and d[0] consists of all zeros.

The state starts as the Initialization Vector, and the first word is then exclusive-ored with the parameter block: h[0] := h[0] ^ 0x01010000 ^ (kk << 8) ^ nn. Every block except the last is compressed with F, passing the offset at the end of that block and the flag FALSE. The last block is compressed with the flag TRUE, and with the offset ll for an unkeyed hash or ll + bb for a keyed one. The digest is the first nn bytes taken from the little-endian word array h.

Appendix A works through the unkeyed hash of the three ASCII bytes abc with BLAKE2b-512, showing internal values during the computation, and Appendix B does the same for BLAKE2s-256. The document notes that, because of space constraints, it does not contain a full set of test vectors for BLAKE2. Reference C implementations for BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s are given in Appendices C and D, and these implementations MAY be validated with the more exhaustive test module in Appendix E.
sections.plainLanguage: To produce a digest, the key and the message are padded into fixed-size blocks and run through the compression function one block at a time. The result is the first nn bytes of the final state, where nn is the digest size the caller asked for.

sections.title: Standard Parameter Sets and Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
An implementation of BLAKE2b and/or BLAKE2s MAY support the listed digest size parameters for interoperability, for example in digital signatures, as long as a sufficient level of security is attained by the parameter selections. These parameters and identifiers are intended to be suitable as drop-in replacements for MD5 and the corresponding SHA algorithms.

For BLAKE2b the identifiers cover digests of 20, 32, 48 and 64 bytes, with collision security of 2^80, 2^128, 2^192 and 2^256. For BLAKE2s they cover 16, 20, 28 and 32 bytes, with collision security of 2^64, 2^80, 2^112 and 2^128. Each identifier also has a suffix in the ASN.1 object identifier tree.

Developers adapting BLAKE2 to ASN.1-based message formats SHOULD use the OID tree at x = 1.3.6.1.4.1.1722.12.2. The same OID can be used for both keyed and unkeyed hashing, since in the latter case the key simply has zero length. The document then gives the full object identifier definitions for the hash algorithms, for the MAC algorithms, and for the individual BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists a set of digest sizes that implementations can agree on, so that different programs produce the same value, and gives each one an identifier for use in ASN.1 messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it is intended to provide convenient open-source access to the BLAKE2 cryptographic hash algorithm, and that it wishes to make no independent assertion about the algorithm's security. Readers are referred to the BLAKE and BLAKE2 papers for the detailed cryptanalytic rationale behind the design.

One practical note concerns the reference implementations in Appendices C and D. To avoid bloat, they may not erase all sensitive data, such as secret keys, immediately from process memory after use. The document says that such cleanup can be added if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not claim that BLAKE2 is secure. It points to the two research papers for that reasoning, and warns that the sample C code may leave a secret key in memory after use.

data.title: Computing a BLAKE2 digest
data.code:
h[0..7] := IV[0..7]
h[0] := h[0] ^ 0x01010000 ^ (kk << 8) ^ nn
IF dd > 1 THEN
  FOR i = 0 TO dd - 2 DO
    h := F( h, d[i], (i + 1) * bb, FALSE )
  END FOR
END IF
IF kk = 0 THEN
  h := F( h, d[dd - 1], ll, TRUE )
ELSE
  h := F( h, d[dd - 1], ll + bb, TRUE )
END IF
RETURN first "nn" bytes from little-endian word array h[]
